Q: Use AFL++ fuzzing on an embedded software working on serial port inputs A:

AFL++ works by compiling your code with a special compiler. Your target isn't supported by that special compiler, so that's indeed a quick end to that setup.

However, you probably should fix your code. Isolate the RS232 part and any other hardware dependency from the parser logic. Next, replace that RS232 part with a simple snippet that reads from stdin, so you can parse that input. Write some regular test cases. You can now use these tests in a proper CI/CD pipeline. But since this test executable is just a regular C99 executable, it can also be fuzzed.

Q: How to implement a social media/website monitoring service? A:

Just focusing on this:

Review sites I looked at some review site's TOS and they wrote that using an automated software crawling their sites is not permitted.

If the TOS says "no crawling", then you shouldn't do that. They would be within their rights to block you / your company from accessing their sites if you violate their TOS. And they may have other remedies!

Note that there are many reasons for banning crawling. One of them is that crawlers cost them money ... for no return to them.

A "get out" would be if what you are proposing doesn't violate the review site's TOS. For example, if you could use a review site's (hypothetical) search APIs to find mentions of your products ... without "crawling" ... that might be acceptable. However that would depend on 1) the precise wording of the TOS, and 2) what you were actually doing and how you were doing it.

Note that we can't give you sound advice on this. It is fundamentally a legal question. Ask an Intellectual Property lawyer. (We aren't lawyers here!!)

On the other hand, the sites that are relevant to me are not disallowed in their robots.txt. What matters here?

  1. The meaning of the robots.txt file is conventional. It has no legal authority.

  2. It depends on what the robots.txt file says. For example, the file could allow some agents and not others.

  3. If there was an apparent contradiction between a site's TOS and their robots.txt, it may be up to a judge and/or jury to decide which one is operative. But you don't want to get to that point because it will cost your company a lot of money (lawyers fees, discovery costs, etc) to fight a civil lawsuit ... even if you win.

In short, BOTH the TOS and the robots.txt matter. If EITHER says don't crawl, then don't crawl. (Unless you / your company is willing to risk an expensive lawsuit. And if you / they are, then talk to your lawyer first!!)

Q: Scraping AirBnb Data, but receiving NA values A:

NA in rvest almost always means the nodes weren't in the HTML you fetched. Airbnb renders listing data client-side, so read_html() only gets the initial React shell and html_element() finds nothing (hence the NAs). rvest can't run the JavaScript, so no CSS/XPath selector will fix it.

Two reliable routes in R:

1. Hit the JSON directly. Open the listing in a browser, DevTools → Network → filter XHR, and find the StaysSearch (search results) or StaysPdpSections / PdpAvailabilityCalendar (single listing) call. Replay it in R and parse the JSON:

library(httr2); library(jsonlite)

resp <- request("https://www.airbnb.com/api/v3/StaysPdpSections/...") |>

req_headers(

\`User-Agent\`      `= "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36",`

\`X-Airbnb-API-Key\``= "<copy the key from that same request>"`

) |>

req_perform()

data <- fromJSON(resp_body_string(resp), flatten = TRUE)

Price, room type, rating and coordinates are already fields in that JSON, so there's nothing to scrape out of HTML.

2. Render first, then scrape. Drive a real browser with RSelenium so the JS runs, wait for the price node, then hand the source to rvest:

library(RSelenium); library(rvest)

remDr$navigate(url)

Sys.sleep(5) # let it render

pg <- read_html(remDr$getPageSource()[[1]])

price <- pg |> html_element("[data-testid='...']") |> html_text2()

Two things that bite people either way: send a real User-Agent (R's default agent gets an empty or blocked page), and don't select by class — Airbnb's class names are hashed and rotate every deploy, so target data-testid or read the JSON. At volume you'll also want rotating residential proxies and delays, since Airbnb rate-limits and throws CAPTCHAs.

Q: UBL Invoice validation: Cannot find the declaration of element 'ubl:Invoice' A:

The error mean the validator has no schema for that namespace Invoice-2. I read the XML itself; seems is good to me. UBL files don't contain xsi:schemaLocation, so you have to tell the validator which XSD to use.

You can download the official UBL 2.1 zip from OASIS (the file UBL-2.1.zip at docs.oasis-open.org/ubl/os-UBL-2.1/), and validate against You should keep the zip folder structure, to avoid import problems with cac/cbc.

I tried the command: xmllint --noout --schema xsd/maindoc/UBL-Invoice-2.1.xsd invoice.xml and got the output:

.../invoice.xml validates

Q: Remove const or get a non-const object A:

"I defined the reference as 'const' because in the most cases ..."

As long as there's at least one case where the referenced object is changed, you should define it as non-const.

Casting away const is technically legal in some situations, but that's pretty rare. In practice, it's used when a method is conceptually const but the implementation isn't. For instance, an expensive getter might implement a cache. Calling the getter logically doesn't change the object, even though it changes an internal cache member.
